prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose and poetry that turn memory, the body and dream into an inner cosmos of metaphysical and historical reach.

statement.case_for: Judged on the common criteria, Cărtărescu's case is the strongest on the shortlist. His voice is immediately recognizable: long, hallucinatory, densely patterned prose in which body, memory and dream become a metaphysical project (Blinding, the first part of the Orbitor trilogy, and Solenoid, on public knowledge). The formal achievement is the construction of large, internally coherent architectures, not ornament. The imaginative and intellectual depth reaches into cosmology, the history of the Romanian twentieth century and the experience of a single consciousness. The oeuvre also has generic breadth, since he began as a poet and writes essays, so the claim covers a body of work and not one celebrated book. The later large novels appear to extend the project rather than repeat it, which supports sustained quality and maturity. A single-writer citation is straightforward. This rests on public knowledge of the works, not on fresh reading or independent verification.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the very scale and density that make the work distinctive may also be its weakness. Over thousands of pages, encyclopedic accumulation and recurring motifs can shade into self-enclosure or repetition, and I cannot verify from public knowledge alone whether the late volumes deepen the project or only enlarge it. Much of the evidence reaches us through translation, which only partly conveys the rhythm and syntax of long Romanian sentences. The poetry and early work are the least covered part of the corpus, so the whole-oeuvre claim is partly inferred from the major novels.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita first. He argues that Purgatory and Anteparadise turn suffering and historical rupture into a distinctive, sustained poetic form, joining private lyric and collective memory, with landscape-scale interventions extending the project beyond the page.
responses.response: I agree that the voice is unmistakable and that the moral and formal seriousness is real. I ranked Zurita second for that reason, and I keep him as an alternative. I qualify two things. The claim rests on a single genre, and poetry of this kind, where sequence, sound and Spanish-language register carry much of the effect, loses the most in translation. Our collective judgment of the translated corpus is therefore the least secure here. Second, I agree with Olsson that the landscape and public interventions should be read as an extension of the written work. If we cannot weigh them as literature, the claim narrows to the page. Cărtărescu also depends on translation, but I think the loss is less total for large-scale prose architecture than for poetry built on sonic and sequential effects. The case for Zurita seems to me more dependent on his historical context than the case for Cărtărescu, and I would want to separate the two.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Yan Lianke second. He values the grotesque, mythic and satirical forms and the poetics of 'mythorealism' as formally inventive, not merely testimonial, and insists that restriction in China must not substitute for merit.
responses.response: I share the principle that censorship and political symbolism do not establish literary merit, and his point that the work is formally inventive is fair. I ranked Yan sixth, not higher. My doubt is about the corpus: it is large and, as translation shows, uneven, and I cannot tell whether the strongest books (The Four Books, The Explosion Chronicles) carry the whole oeuvre or whether the translated selection flatters it. Sem-Sandberg is more persuasive on the poetics than I was in my opening, and that is a reason to keep Yan under discussion. It does not yet move him above a candidate whose formal project seems to me both more consistent and more fully realized.

responses.point: Mattson ranks NDiaye second, citing controlled, uncanny prose on exclusion, family power and unstable belonging in Three Strong Women and My Heart Hemmed In, with drama broadening the range, and notes that her output is more compact than the largest on the list.
responses.response: I agree that NDiaye's disciplined economy and tonal control are a distinctive achievement, and that her command of estrangement across fiction and plays is real. We differ on weighting. I ranked her fifth. Her oeuvre is established and still developing, but the question I cannot resolve from public knowledge is whether its breadth and cumulative weight match the imaginative scale of the strongest candidates. Mattson names the compactness too. Her syntax and tonal precision are also exactly the qualities translation tends to flatten, and the drama is less well covered abroad. I would be glad to hear which of her works Mattson sees as carrying the main claim.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Adonis third. She sees the remaking of Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and dialogue with inherited forms as an achievement concerning a whole literary language, with the essays adding intellectual depth.
responses.response: I accept that the formal and linguistic significance within Arabic poetry is large and that the essays are part of the same project. I ranked him seventh, and the reason is evidentiary. The achievement lies in prosody and the relation to classical forms, which is exactly what translation conveys least, so a judgment of the whole depends heavily on a few translated volumes. I also see an open question about how to weigh the essays against the poetry in a citation. Carlberg is right that his historical weight is not in doubt. My reservation is whether our ability to judge the poems as poems is sufficient, not whether the work matters.

uncertainties: My assessment of all candidates rests on public knowledge of the works. I have not read texts in this session or independently verified any source.
Whether the late, very large Cărtărescu volumes deepen the project or enlarge it by repetition cannot be settled from the supplied evidence.

Translation carries much of the evidence for Cărtărescu, and even more for the poetry candidates (Zurita, Adonis), so the committee's reading of the originals may differ from what translations suggest.
Corpus coverage is uneven: Cărtărescu's poetry, essays and early work, and NDiaye's drama, are less well known to me than the major novels.
How far Zurita's landscape-scale and performative interventions count as literary achievement within Nobel's framework is unresolved.
Alexis Wright's oeuvre is relatively compact, so sustained quality over a large corpus is harder to judge, and the committee may weigh timing differently.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own work on Selma Lagerlöf and my fiction are context and not evidence of favoring any candidate, and I do not infer a personal tie to any shortlisted writer from my profile.
